stance_basis: opens letter calling draft statement 'totally inadequate' and demanding its withdrawal
summary: Greg E. Studen, co-signatory of a letter from Grey & Studen on behalf of the Natural Resources Defense Council, argues that the draft Environmental Impact Statement is totally inadequate and fails to comply with NEPA, Executive Order 11644, and other applicable laws. He demands that both the draft statement and the Secretary's May 16 memorandum be withdrawn and that the entire implementation process begin again. The attached NRDC comments elaborate extensively on the statement's deficiencies, including its failure to identify and protect environmental values, its accommodation of ORV use over environmental protection, and its inconsistency with statutes governing national parks and wildlife refuges.
complaint_summary: The attached NRDC comments detail multiple deficiencies in the draft EIS, including its failure to identify the proposal it accompanies, its failure to comply with NEPA's and EO 11644's environmental protection objectives, and its inconsistency with statutes governing national parks and wildlife refuges, arguing that ORV use must be strictly regulated and banned from parks and refuges.

statement.text:
Comments of
Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc.

on Interior Department Draft Environmental

Impact Statement Regarding

Off-Road Vehicle Use

I. Background and Introduction
On February 9, 1972, President Nixon issued Executive Order 11644 (37 F.R. 2877), noting a rapid increase in the use of off-road vehicles (ORVs) on public lands and recognizing that ORV use conflicts with resource conservation, environmental values, and other recreational uses of the public domain. The President called for a "unified Federal policy" towards ORV use on public land -- a policy that would regulate ORV use to protect resources, promote the safety of all users of public lands, and minimize the conflicts between users. Executive Order 11644 directs agency heads with jurisdiction over public lands to specify areas as open or closed to ORV use, and issue regulations prescribing operating conditions on open areas.
The Secretary of the Interior's memorandum of May 5, 1972, implements E.O. 11644. It directs Assistant Secretaries to review existing regulations governing ORV use on lands under their jurisdictions, to categorize all lands as either open or closed to ORV use, and to recommend for adoption regulations that will protect resources and minimize conflicts between ORVs and other uses of the public lands. The memorandum also requires appropriate Interior Bureaus to submit regulations and administrative guidelines that will implement the Executive Order on the lands which they administer.
Interior's proposed implementation of E.O. 11644 is accompanied by the Draft Impact Statement on Off-Road Vehicles. This statement is intended to satisfy the requirement of the National Environmental

Policy Act for a "detailed statement" of the environmental impacts of proposals for "major Federal actions significantly affecting the quality of the human environment." NEPA requires the statement to include a discussion of unavoidable adverse effects, alternatives, effects on long-term productivity, and irreversible commitments of resources which are involved in the proposed action. In order to satisfy the requirements of NEPA, and to effectively implement the purposes of the Executive Order, the draft statement on off-road vehicles should identify clearly the values that deserve protection on the public lands and document precisely the impact of ORV use on those values.
Unfortunately, the Draft Statement fails completely to carry out the clear mandate of NEPA and E.O. 11644. It is a nebulous document that only confuses and weakens Interior's attempt to fulfill its responsibilities. As a result, it seriously misdirects the effort to preserve and enhance environmental quality on the public lands. This comment will discuss the deficiencies that make the Draft Statement so weak, and will suggest a new approach for a more forthright policy of environmental protection.
II. Defects of the Draft Statement
A. Failure to indicate the proposal which it accompanies.
According to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), sec. 102(2)(c), an impact statement must "accompany" proposals for "major Federal actions significantly affecting the quality of the environment." But what is the proposal that the Draft Impact Statement accompanies? It can hardly be a proposal for actual

land-use classifications or Interior regulations, since no such actions have yet been proposed, and it is therefore impossible to assess their impacts. We must conclude that the Statement is intended to accompany the Secretary's decision to implement the President's order according to his May 5 memorandum. If the Statement is to function as intended, however, the Secretary must be willing to treat his memorandum as announcing a "proposal", not a final decision, and revise it on the basis of comments and a final impact statement. Otherwise the Draft Statement is a meaningless gesture which plays no useful role.
The draft statement itself only confuses further the issue of what action it is intended to accompany. The statement does not describe any concrete "proposal" with regard to ORVs. It is merely a general policy statement which points out that ORV use does affect the environment. This is by no means a "detailed statement" of the impact of regulations to be proposed in the future. When proposals are made for specific regulations dealing with particular lands, NEPA requires that they be accompanied by detailed statements which identify their impacts. For the present, we will assume that the Secretary's memorandum is the "proposal" that this draft statement accompanies and that the memorandum is subject to change.
B. Failure to comply with the objectives of NEPA and E.O. 11644.
Although the draft statement's basic purpose is unclear, it would be useful if it at least stated a forthright policy of protection for environmental values on the public lands. Protecting the values of the natural environment is one of the clear purposes

of NEPA. Section 101(a) of the Act declares,
The Congress, recognizing the profound impact of man's activity on the interrelations of all components of the natural environment, particularly the profound influences of population growth, high density urbanization, industrial expansion, resource exploitation, and new and expanding technological advances ... declares that it is the continuing policy of the Federal Government ... to use all practical means and measures ... to create and maintain conditions under which man and nature can exist in productive harmony, and fulfill the social, economic, and other requirements of present and future generations of Americans.
One of the means by which this policy is implemented is the environmental impact statement required by sec. 102(2)(c) of the Act. In order to function meaningfully, an impact statement must take account of basic environmental values, and document precisely the way in which they are threatened or enhanced by the proposed action under consideration.
Executive Order 11644 notes that ORVs are used "... in frequent conflict with wise land and resource management practices, environmental values, and other types of recreational activity ..."

The purpose of the order, explicitly stated in sec. 1, is to
... ensure that the use of off-road vehicles on public lands will be controlled and directed so as to protect the resources of those lands, to promote the safety of all users of those lands, and to minimize the conflicts among the uses of those lands.
The Executive Order refers again to these purposes in section 3, directing that they form the basis for administrative designation of zones which will be open or closed to ORV use. These purposes make explicit the duty of the Interior Department to identify the values of the public lands that deserve protection from the impacts of ORV.

ORVs must be strictly regulated because they bring the noise, smells, and potential destructiveness of modern mechanical civilization into areas where undisturbed nature predominates. These areas, where the natural world is at least relatively free from destructive mechanical impacts, are an important national They offer opportunities for wildlife, soil, and water conservation, for informal and scientific nature study, and for recreational use. In them people may find undisturbed vegetation and wildlife, solitude, and natural beauty. However, these values can easily be destroyed by overuse or misure and the areas where they may be found have been rapidly dwindling in size. Because of their destructive impacts and great mobility ORVs are a particularly serious threat. As the draft statement itself points out, "Land, water, air, wildlife, and vegetation resources will be detrimentally affected in areas of ORV use." (p. 24) If the values of natural areas are to be preserved and protected, ORV use will have to be strictly regulated.
In many cases, lands administered by the Interior Department offer great opportunities for the protection and enjoyment of the values offered by an undisturbed environment. These values have been given recognition and protection by NEPA and E.O. 11644. Yet nowhere in the Draft Statement does Interior indicate anything more than a brief formal recognition that these values exist. Even then the values of natural areas and the limited levels of recreational use compatible with the protection of the resource base seem to be weighed lightly against the notion that the Department must accommodate all demands for use. As a result, the

statement communicates only a faint concern for the real dangers to the natural environment posed by ORVs. Because it fails to distinguish clearly between ORVs, which impair the basic resources of public lands, and other recreational activities which have a minimal effect on the environment, the draft statement creates an overall impression of anti-environmental bias. It suggests that a fuzzy sort of accommodation with ORV use is the guiding principle of Interior policy. This conflicts with the intent of E.O. 11644, NEPA, and the fundamental mission of the Interior Department to protect resources for all Americans, now and in the future. Interior's clear duty is not to accede to all demands for use of public resources but only to those that do not impair basic values.
C. Failure to comply with other laws which provide for protection of the natural environment and recreational resources of public lands.
The Interior Department's legal mandate in managing public lands is set forth in a number of statutes. From these statutes it is clear that there are some lands where any use which is as damaging as ORVs must not be allowed at all by the Department.

Among these lands are the national parks and the national wildlife refuges. The act establishing the National Park Service, 16 USC 1, provides that the Service shall manage the national parks, monuments, and reservations
by such means and measures as conform to [their] fundamental purpose ..., which purpose is to conserve the scenery and the natural and historic objects and the wildlife therein and to provide for the enjoyment of the same in such manner and by such means as will leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations.

Section 20 of 16 USC provides a further statement of the basic purpose of the national parks:
... these areas [the national park system] are united through their interrelated purposes and resources into one national park system ... preserved and managed for the benefit and inspiration of all the people of the United States.
These statutes make improper any use of the parks that impairs their basic natural resources. Although the draft statement leaves no doubt that ORV use does substantially impair resources wherever it is allowed,* the Secretary's memo states that ORV areas will be allowed in the Park System if the bureau head determines that "off-road vehicle use ... will not adversely affect ... natural, aesthetic, or scenic values." This is plainly inconsistent with the Draft Statement's declaration that ORV use always adversely affects natural values. Consequently, the Secretary should change his memo to require that ORVs be banned from national park lands.
Recreational use within the National Wildlife Refuge System is controlled by 16 USC 460k. That section provides that recreational use within the refuge system or in other conservation areas administered by the Secretary of the Interior for fish and wildlife purposes, will be allowed if such use can be made compatible with the primary purpose of the conservation areas, and can be an appropriate secondary or incidental use. The draft statement makes clear that ORV use is incompatible with wildlife
*
The statement mentions several impacts on pages 11-17, and states on p.12 that "Even when properly operated, the impact may be great and, in many instances, irretrievable on individually-designated areas."

conservation. On page 31, the Statement points out that "natural areas of the National Park System and of the National Wildlife Refuge System would have their basic program missions compromised if ORV use were permitted on them." This conclusion is supported by Interior's own Off-road Recreation Vehicle Task Force Study, which states on page 30, "ORV use ... is basically incompatible with the primary purpose of the Refuge System." Therefore the Secretary's memorandum, which allows ORV use on the Wildlife Refuges if the responsible bureau head determines that the use will not damage resources, should be changed to forbid ORV use in these areas.
On other lands administered by the Department, the Classification and Multiple Use Act of 1964, 43 USC 1411-18, requires that the Secretary classify retained Federal lands by use category. Among the uses permitted for retained lands are " ... (6) outdoor recreation ... or (10) preservation of public values that would be lost if the land passed from Federal ownership." 43 USC 1411(a) In making determinations, the Secretary is required to " ... give due consideration to all pertinent factors, including but not limited to, ecology, priorities of use, and the relative values of the various resources in particular areas." 43 USC 1411(b)
Use priorities are necessary whenever lands are suitable for incompatible uses; e.g., ORV use and wildlife study. These priorities must take account of the environmental impacts of the competing uses, and give preference to uses which do not impair basic environmental values.
